extracted.intended_audience: scientists, journal editors, programme managers, research evaluators, and policymakers involved in peer review and research assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, conducting, and interpreting peer review of scientific work (manuscripts, grant applications, research groups, and teaching), including its linkage with bibliometric indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and function of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is used to ensure the quality of manuscripts and to legitimise scientific work; it determines publication, awarding of grants, jobs, prizes, and evaluations of research groups and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review should act as a filter 'to separate the wheat from the chaff' and to guarantee and improve quality; historically served to render results trustworthy (e.g., by repeating experiments or critically reviewing descriptions). It is used both ex ante (planned research, applications) and ex post (completed research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability across evaluation contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is applicable to manuscripts, grant applications, prizes, jobs, institutional and group evaluations, and teaching/education assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The arrangements (e.g., criteria, number of referees, anonymity) can vary substantially across and within these application areas; evaluators should choose designs appropriate to the specific context and aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of formalisation of evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation can follow highly formalised specifications or leave selection of criteria to the referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must decide whether to impose standardised criteria or allow expert discretion; trade-offs include comparability and standardisation versus context-sensitive judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee and author anonymity (blinding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees may be anonymous or named; authors may be identifiable or anonymised (single-blind vs double-blind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of blinding affects bias, fairness, and transparency. The review notes the existence of these variants but implies implications for fairness and possible biases in outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of referees and independence vs group deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluation can be performed by one or several referees; groups can evaluate independently or collaboratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using multiple referees and independent assessments can affect reliability; group deliberation may produce different dynamics. Designers should consider how many experts and which interaction mode best serve the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee appointment: permanent versus ad hoc
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees can be appointed on a permanent basis (standing panels) or assembled ad hoc for individual evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent panels may increase consistency or entrenchment; ad hoc selection may increase flexibility or variability. Consider conflicts of interest and panel expertise in each model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accessibility versus confidentiality of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can be designed to be public (open) or confidential (closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openness affects transparency and accountability; confidentiality may encourage candid assessments. Designers must balance transparency with potential chilling effects and privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core referee tasks: selection, improvement, error detection, integrity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are tasked to recommend the 'best' research given scarce resources, formulate suggestions for improvement, find errors in scientific work, and identify incorrect scientific conduct associated with the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should both guide selection and offer constructive feedback; they also function as a mechanism to detect scientific errors and misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability (inter-referee agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether different referees agree in their assessment of the same scientific work (consistency/reliability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics observe lack of reliability — different referees often disagree. Consider designs (number of referees, standard criteria) and measurement to improve reliability or to account for variability in decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and systematic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which recommendations are free from systematic bias and based only on scientific quality rather than non-scientific criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms highlight that work is sometimes judged on non-scientific criteria (lack of fairness). Measures such as blinding, diverse reviewer pools, and use of objective indicators can mitigate bias but have trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity (correspondence with true quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The correlation between peer review judgements and the actual quality of the refereed work (validity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics claim low correlation between peer judgements and true quality. The review suggests combining methods (e.g., bibliometrics) and improving rigour in peer-review studies to better assess validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of active scientists as referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents consider active scientists in the same field the most suitable people to evaluate scientific quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active practitioners bring relevant expertise and disciplinary standards; however, using peers creates reciprocal dynamics that may standardise criteria or introduce conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardisation and norm propagation through peer systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Because scientists are both referees and refereed, peer review contributes to standardising evaluation criteria and formal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative effect can help harmonise standards across a field but may also suppress heterodox approaches; be mindful of tension between standardisation and intellectual diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive selection versus negative selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between negative selection (filtering out work below a minimum standard) and positive selection (choosing the best among many good submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive selection requires finer discriminations and increases the likelihood of rejecting projects that may later prove successful; it demands higher demands on reviewers and the evaluation system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed peer review: linking bibliometrics to peer judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to use an informed peer review process where peers have access to bibliometric indicators that inform but do not replace judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliometrics should complement peer review. If comprehensive and sound, they inform reviewers and strengthen transparency and substantiation of decisions; they are not a substitute for expert assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliometrics as verification and anti-network safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric indicators can subject peer evaluations to verification and help protect decisions from 'old boys' network' effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics provide an external check on subjective judgements; designers should ensure indicators are appropriate and used to verify rather than deterministically decide outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert interpretation and context-awareness of indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric results require interpretation by expert referees; direct evaluation according to context-independent indicators is impossible without relevance specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators should be annotated, enhanced and corrected by experts who understand disciplinary and contextual nuances; avoid decontextualised, formalised metric-only assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined-method benefits and balancing trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Using both peer review and bibliometrics allows reviewers to compare subjective judgment with quantitative indicators, balancing pros and cons depending on context and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combination can lead to more comprehensive evaluations; weight of each method should depend on evaluation objectives and context. Studies show positive correlation between peer esteem and citation frequency in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluator workload, timeliness, and increasing demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees, editors and programme managers face increased demands: they must now select the best from many high-quality submissions, not just filter out poor work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increased workload affects timeliness and the capacity for thorough review. Systems should account for reviewer time constraints and consider incentives, triage mechanisms, or support (e.g., bibliometrics) to aid decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards for peer review research
rubrics_metrics.description: Much research on peer review has been opinion-based rather than rigorous empirical study; there is a need for higher rigour in studying peer review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or reforming peer review, base decisions on rigorous evidence rather than editorials or anecdote; evaluate interventions with proper research designs.
